extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science, philosophers of science, and scientists interested in scientific method and the character of experimentalists
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the intellectual and practical qualities that constitute a strong experimental scientist: reasoning method (hypothesis-testing), experimental skill, imagination, candour, tenacity, and judgment, as presented in a philosophy-of-science textbook excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental skill and invention of simple qualitative experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Faraday was probably equal to Newton in experimental skill, and in that peculiar kind of deductive power which leads to the invention of simple qualitative experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value simplicity and inventiveness in apparatus; the experimentalist should be able to make a few simple pieces of apparatus give deep results. Example: Newton made simple apparatus yield unsuspected depths of meaning; Faraday's patient labours and varied experiments (including many failures) illustrate high experimental skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical power for following out quantitative consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton exhibited mathematical power which enabled him to follow out intuitively the quantitative results of complicated problems with wonderful facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experimentalists who can combine experimental ingenuity with mathematical analysis to derive and test quantitative consequences; lack of mathematical power limits ability to pursue complex quantitative problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newtonian (hypothetico-deductive) method / Novum Organum
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton's method develops the methods of deductive reasoning and experimental verification: from a series of inductions we may rise to causes of phenomena, and then descend again to all the resulting details. The Principia forms the true 'Novum Organum' of scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses must be definite in conditions and admit unquestionable deductive reasoning; the value of each hypothesis is decided by comparing its consequences with facts. The method: imagine causes, deduce consequences, compare with experiment. Examples: Newton's exhaustive treatment of many laws and cases; Archimedes as antecedent Organum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-guides-experiment (theory should suggest decisive tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory should guide experiment: 'theory guiding experiment, and yet wholly relying on experiment for confirmation.' Newton invented experiments by mathematically determining phenomena; Huyghens calculated expected results and then checked them with observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to test precise consequences of theories; use theory to invent decisive, simple tests (e.g., Newton's prism and refraction experiments; Huyghens' predicted refraction behaviors in crystals). Avoid aimless or purely accidental experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness of hypotheses and exhaustive consideration of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: No hypothesis is entertained unless it is definite in conditions and admits of unquestionable deductive reasoning; Newton ran rapidly over many suppositions and drew consequences from each, selecting the one that yields results agreeing with experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate hypotheses with clear conditions that permit deductive derivation of observable consequences; consider alternative hypotheses and derive consequences for each so experiments can discriminate among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour and readiness to reject theories inconsistent with fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect readiness to reject a theory inconsistent with fact is a primary requisite of the philosophic mind; there must be scrupulous honesty and flexibility of mind which assigns adequate value to all evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cling to favored theories in the face of contrary evidence; weigh all evidence impartially. Example: value placed on willingness to abandon theories when decisive contrary facts are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pertinacity and courage in maintaining a hypothesis until conclusively falsified
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness to reject a false theory may be combined with a peculiar pertinacity and courage in maintaining an hypothesis as long as its falsity is not actually apparent; when a theory exhibits striking coincidences with fact it must not be thrown aside until at least one conclusive discordance is proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain promising theories tenaciously while actively seeking decisive tests; avoid abandoning theories at the first difficulty but also do not refuse to abandon them when conclusive contrary evidence appears. Example: Leslie's description of warm and obstinate defence leading to relinquishment only after being driven from every post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience with negative results and iterative re-experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of Faraday's experiments gave negative results, yet he concluded 'the experiments were well made, but the results are negative; I cannot accept them as conclusive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat negative or null results as informative but not necessarily definitive; revisit experimental design, sensitivity, and controls, and re-examine whether the effect might be too slight or arrangements unsuited. Persevere in reworking experiments when justified by theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of bias and suspension (reservation) of judgment when data are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another characteristic needed: suspending judgment when the data are insufficient. The exercise of the judgment ought to end in absolute reservation; we ought to be cautious because we are not infallible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid premature confident opinions; the philosophic mind often remains in doubt until sufficient evidence accumulates. Example: Arago declined to put forward any public theory after discovering a phenomenon until its conditions were well investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of fertile theorising with strict empirical verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind of the great discoverer must combine contradictory attributes: be fertile in theories and hypotheses, and yet full of facts and precise results of experience; entertain feeble analogies and guesses, yet hold them worthless until verified in experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage speculative imagination to generate hypotheses but require rigorous experimental tests before acceptance. Maintain imagination 'guarded by judgment and principle' and 'directing it by experiment' (Faraday).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of similarities, generalisation, and proper use of analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific reasoning consists in inferring of a thing what we know of similar objects; all induction implies generalisation. In practice we detect similarities and then assume (roughly) that similars in some respects are similars in others when precise data are lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogical reasoning cautiously: ascend to general propositions where warranted rather than infer directly from particular to particular; when precise probability data are absent, make controlled assumptions about similarity and state their uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and exhaustiveness in exploring consequences of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: What strikes the reader is the exhaustiveness of [Newton's] treatment, and the unbounded power of his insight; he investigates many, or almost all imaginable laws and sketches results of each. He follows consequences of a preconceived theory into every consequence and tests them by a variety of simple comparisons with fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a hypothesis, work out as many observable consequences as feasible and test them; exhaustive consideration increases confidence in a theory and yields many opportunities for decisive testing.
